extracted.intended_audience: Registered patent agents and attorneys, trademark practitioners, and other persons who practice or seek to practice before the USPTO (including law clinic supervisors and law students participating in USPTO programs).
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, rules, procedures, and eligibility criteria governing practice before the USPTO, including discipline, conflicts, signature requirements, diversion eligibility, and related administrative obligations. Useful for attorneys/agents to comply with USPTO ethical and procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED Diversion Pilot Program eligibility — willingness and ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must have willingness and ability to participate in the Diversion Pilot Program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program launched 2017 and extended; participation may be allowed even with prior discipline in some circumstances. This is an eligibility gate for diversion as an alternative to formal discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED Diversion Pilot Program disqualifying misconduct types
rubrics_metrics.description: Misconduct at issue must not involve misappropriation of funds or dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation; must not result in or be likely to result in substantial prejudice to a client or other person; must not constitute a 'serious crime'; must not be part of a pattern of major similar misconduct or be of the same nature as misconduct for which practitioner has been disciplined within the past five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These restrictions limit which matters are eligible for diversion; see 37 C.F.R. § 11.1 for definition of 'serious crime.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of practice before the Office (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.5(b) & 11.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities constituting practice before the USPTO include communicating with and advising a client concerning matters pending or contemplated to be presented before the Office and consulting with or giving advice in contemplation of filing patent or trademark applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also permits practitioners to employ or retain non-practitioner assistants under supervision; see 37 C.F.R. § 11.14 for who may practice in trademark and non-patent matters. This definition determines who is subject to USPTO professional rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance definition and initiation of investigation (37 C.F.R. § 11.22(a) & §11.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A grievance is a written submission from any source received by the OED Director that presents possible grounds for discipline of a specified practitioner; receipt of a grievance may initiate an investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During investigation the OED Director may request information from the grievant, the practitioner, or any person reasonably expected to provide information or evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.22(f)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible OED outcomes after investigation (37 C.F.R. § 11.22(h))
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon conclusion of an investigation, the OED Director may close the investigation without action, issue a warning, institute formal charges (with Committee on Discipline approval), or enter into a settlement agreement and submit it to the USPTO Director for approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the procedural dispositions available at investigation conclusion; formal charges require Committee review/approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral to Committee on Discipline and probable cause determination (37 C.F.R. § 11.32)
rubrics_metrics.description: If investigation reveals grounds for discipline, the matter may be referred to the Committee on Discipline to make a probable cause determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referral is the step toward formal proceedings; Committee then assesses whether probable cause exists to proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing limits for filing complaints (37 C.F.R. § 11.34(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: A complaint shall be filed within one year after the date on which the OED Director receives a grievance; no complaint may be filed more than 10 years after the date on which the misconduct occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute of limitations-style filing windows for OED complaints; be aware both the one-year and ten-year limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-reporting as mitigating factor in discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-reporting of misconduct is often considered mitigating in the disciplinary process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-reporting can influence disposition and sanctions, potentially reducing severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal discipline procedures (37 C.F.R. § 11.24)
rubrics_metrics.description: OED may impose reciprocal discipline based on discipline by a state or federal program or agency; such matters are often conducted on the documentary record only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciprocal discipline does not require re-litigating underlying facts in many cases; it implements discipline imposed elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim suspension on conviction of serious crime (37 C.F.R. § 11.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may face interim suspension based on conviction of a serious crime; matters are referred to a hearing officer for determination of final disciplinary action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interim suspension protects the public while final determination is made; see rule for definitions and procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest — concurrent conflict prohibition (37 C.F.R. § 11.107(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not represent a client if the representation involves a concurrent conflict of interest: (1) representation of one client will be directly adverse to another client; or (2) there is a significant risk that representation will be materially limited by duties to another client, a former client, a third person, or a personal interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the basic prohibition on concurrent conflicts; it applies broadly to USPTO practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict exceptions and required conditions (37 C.F.R. § 11.107(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding a concurrent conflict, a practitioner may represent multiple clients if (1) the practitioner reasonably believes competent and diligent representation to each client is possible; (2) the representation is not prohibited by law; (3) the representation does not involve one client asserting a claim against another before a tribunal; and (4) each affected client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All four conditions must be satisfied to permit representation despite a conflict; obtaining informed written consent is crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting compensation from third parties (37 C.F.R. § 11.108(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not accept compensation for representing a client from one other than the client unless: (1) the client gives informed consent; (2) there is no interference with the practitioner's independence of professional judgment or the client-practitioner relationship; and (3) information relating to representation is protected as required by §11.106.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When third-party payers are involved, ensure written informed consent and safeguard independence and confidentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on allowing third-party payer to direct professional judgment (37 C.F.R. § 11.504(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not permit a person who recommends, employs, or pays the practitioner to direct or regulate the practitioner's professional judgment in rendering legal services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a third party pays, the practitioner's independent judgment must remain unimpaired; failure can lead to discipline (examples provided in case summaries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility regarding non-practitioner assistance (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.503 & 11.503(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners may employ non-practitioner assistants but must take reasonable steps to supervise them and ensure compliance with the rules (e.g., correct signature practices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (Sapp, Lou, Caraco) highlight failures to supervise assistants and resulting discipline; supervision includes training and oversight and notifying clients/USPTO of problems when discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence requirement (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall provide competent representation requiring the legal, scientific, and technical knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence is foundational; lack of competence (e.g., practicing in an unfamiliar area, failing to supervise filings) is a frequent basis for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of representation and communication of fees (37 C.F.R. § 11.102 & §11.105(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must communicate the scope of representation and the basis or rate of fees and expenses; informed consent is required when limiting the scope of representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When limiting services (e.g., prepare-but-not-prosecute), obtain informed consent (see 11.102(c) and 11.105(b)); failure to communicate scope/fee arrangements can create ethics violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor toward the tribunal (37 C.F.R. § 11.303)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not knowingly make false statements of fact or law to a tribunal or fail to correct a false statement; must not offer evidence known to be false and must inform a tribunal of material facts in an ex parte proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes duties to correct prior false statements and to take remedial measures (including disclosure) if material evidence is found false; violations carry severe sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misconduct definitions — dishonesty, prejudice to administration of justice, and related provisions (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c), (d), (i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Misconduct includes dishonesty, fraud, deceit, misrepresentation (11.804(c)), conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (11.804(d)), and other conduct adversely reflecting on fitness to practice (11.804(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions are invoked repeatedly in case highlights (fabricating emails, false statements, fee misconduct); violations frequently lead to suspension or exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence and promptness in representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must act with diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to file or track deadlines (e.g., failing to pay USPTO fees resulting in abandonment) can lead to discipline (see Chirnomas, Kroll).

rubrics_metrics.name: Client communication duties (37 C.F.R. § 11.104)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must communicate effectively with clients, including notifying them of filings, problems, and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases show failures to notify clients of improper signatures, abandoned applications, or material issues resulted in sanctions; cooperation and remedial steps can mitigate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safekeeping property and protecting client interests on termination (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.115 & 11.116)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must keep client funds separate, maintain records, and protect client interests upon termination of representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commingling client funds (holding client fees in personal accounts) and failing to preserve client property are serious violations (see Kroll, Chirnomas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification upon filing of papers (37 C.F.R. § 11.18 & 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: The presentation (signing, filing, submitting) of any document constitutes a certification under §11.18(b); violations of §11.18(b) may jeopardize application/registration validity and may result in sanctions under §11.18(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signatures carry certification obligations; false certification or submission of improperly signed documents can lead to discipline and jeopardize client rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent document signature requirements (37 C.F.R. § 1.4(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Each piece of correspondence requiring a person's signature must be an original handwritten signature in permanent dark ink or a direct/indirect copy of an original; if a copy is filed, the original should be retained as evidence of authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: S-signature rules (1.4(d)(2)) require the signer to insert their own S-signature and certify (1.4(d)(4)(ii)) that the inserted signature is their own. Note regulatory changes (removal of §1.4(e) for certain correspondence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark signature and electronic signature requirements (37 C.F.R. § 2.193 & TMEP § 611.01(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark correspondence that requires a signature must bear a handwritten signature personally signed in permanent ink or an electronic signature personally entered by the named signatory; electronic signatures must be personally entered between forward slashes or use another Director-specified form. TMEP requires practitioners to personally enter electronic signature elements; others may not sign for a qualified practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typing another person's electronic signature is not valid; non-practitioner staff may not sign the practitioner's name. Improper signature practices have led to suspensions, exclusions, and reprimands (multiple case examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on fee-sharing with non-practitioners and duty to inquire (Mikhailova guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a non-practitioner third party refers inventors and collects payments, the practitioner must question the inventor and referring party about amounts charged to ensure entire practitioner compensation is remitted; otherwise practitioner may have impermissibly shared fees with a non-practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner cannot blindly accept referrals and payments; must investigate fee arrangements and avoid undisclosed fee-sharing with non-practitioners (risk of discipline).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to independently assess suitability of representation when referred by third party
rubrics_metrics.description: When a non-practitioner refers inventors for paid patent legal services, the practitioner may not merely 'fill a purchase order' but must independently assess the suitability of sought patent protection and communicate assessment to the inventor; should obtain copies of documents exchanged between company and inventor to determine whether the company is engaging in practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passive acceptance of referrals can create de facto partnerships with non-practitioners or assist in unauthorized practice of law; practitioners must actively evaluate client needs and conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local counsel rule for trademarks (final rule effective Aug 3, 2019)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign-domiciled trademark applicants, registrants, and parties to TTAB proceedings must be represented at the USPTO by an attorney licensed to practice law in the United States; Canadian patent agents may no longer represent Canadian parties in U.S. trademark matters (they may serve only as additionally appointed practitioners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clients must appoint U.S.-licensed counsel for formal responses; USPTO will correspond only with U.S.-licensed attorneys. This change mitigates fraudulent or inaccurate claims of use and improper representation by foreign-domiciled parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper signature conduct and discipline (case-based examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Signing clients' names, allowing non-practitioner assistants to sign, permitting others to insert electronic signatures, or failing to supervise assistants can result in public reprimand, suspension, exclusion, probation, and education requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Starkweather (three-year suspension), Sapp (public reprimand and probation), Lou (three-month suspension), Caraco (exclusion). Mitigating factors (cooperation, no prior discipline) and aggravating factors (prior discipline, lack of remorse) affect sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of deceit, neglect, unauthorized practice and related misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct such as fabricating communications, altering client files without authorization, neglecting matters (failing to file leading to abandonment), offering misleading guarantees, continuing to practice while suspended, commingling funds, and purchasing client referrals can result in heavy sanctions including exclusion and lengthy suspensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple case summaries (Kroll, Chirnomas, others) illustrate types of misconduct and applicable rules (e.g., 10.23, 11.18, 11.115, 11.804) and the severity of consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative/practical requirements — Biennial registration statement & CLE certification
rubrics_metrics.description: Final rule (published Aug 3, 2020) replaces survey with a biennial registration statement; anticipated implementation Nov 2024. Voluntary certification of CLE: certification of six credits within preceding 24 months (5 credits in patent law and practice, 1 credit in ethics) may be recognized in the online practitioner directory (see 37 C.F.R. § 11.11(a)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No active patent practitioner fee; notice will be provided 120 days before due date. CLE ethics credit recognition was delayed indefinitely in presentation notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating and aggravating factors affecting disciplinary outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors such as prior disciplinary history, acceptance of responsibility, cooperation with OED, length of practice, acknowledgment of lapses, and remedial actions (retraining, terminating improper relationships) influence sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case highlights show mitigation (cooperation, lack of prior discipline, remedial steps) can reduce sanctions; aggravating factors (prior discipline, dishonesty, pattern of misconduct) increase severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of OED disciplinary decisions and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions imposing public discipline are available in the FOIA Reading Room and the Official Gazette for Trademarks; resources include www.uspto.gov/oed and trademark Official Gazette links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners can review OED decisions to understand precedents and guidance for compliant practice.
